speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Yeah. Now I feel safe in Troy. No, just since the day of your year.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: In those days, was it safe in Troy?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh, they used to... I guess there was one man who got shot here in Troy.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Yeah?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Who they were telling you about. No, there wasn't much going on.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Oh, you mean Marshall Hayes?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Yeah, that's why. That's why I heard that.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you ever get to meet him? Boy, those are pretty clothes. Your mother made all those, huh?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh, yeah, she made all the clothes. She made a lot of quilts and... She knew how to make everything. Let's take care of all the quilts she used to make. Oh, yeah.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: How about your father's clothes? Did she make those too?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh, no… she didn't make shirts, I don't think. She made dresses. I don't think she made shirts for the boys. And not the suits. A lot of women makes the shirts for the men, too. Yes, they make them. A lot of women likes to make their own shirts for the men. Yeah, my sister does. For her husband, not me. My mother used to make sure the clothes were better than my boys when they were little. You didn't have much to put down in the paper there.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Oh, you're doing fine. You're doing great. I was wondering, does your mom ever tell you any fairy tales or stories from the old country?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: I don't think my mother was. She wasn't that kind. She didn't tell us much of anything. I believe you, too.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: She didn't, huh?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: I remember when I was a good-night. In the monthlies, I was scared to death. Oh. Yeah. Oh, she didn't tell us much. We never asked mother much about anything. About how she looked when she was scared of nothing. I don't know if we really know much about her. She's a quiet woman. Well, I remember she told us very much. We didn't ask her, either.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: How about your dad? Did you get to talk to him a lot?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh, he used to be a lively man. He used to play lively in them. My father used to be more lively than my mother. My mother, she was kind of quiet. My father used to be lively at least, yeah. So he heard. No, they didn't tell us very much. I'd say my brother down there, if you could talk to him, he'd tell you all kinds of things.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: He was telling us about a man that lived out on the ridge named Big Anderson.

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh, yeah. He lived down below, down by the quick fire place. He was a big man from walking down with a big long stick. Oh, he had a long stick. He couldn't get his legs in so bad. He walked with a big long stick in the fire place every Sunday when he went to church. Oh. He used to stop in the fireplace and eat dinner and eat drinks. We had to work in the soul midst. That's not all they could do up there. We had the soul midst. They were pretty young when they went to work. We had to get out and do some work, do some housework.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Now, was this to keep the family going?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Just to keep the family going. But everybody up there did the same thing.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Now, when you went fishing and did the fishing, you were real young then?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh, yes. We as kids, we as young.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you have other kids?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: We went to school. As soon as we were old enough, we could go run around, you know.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you do other things besides fishing?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: I'm kind of surprised to hear that girls went fishing. Oh, yes. We all go fishing. We'd go and pick up the berries up in the woods and my folks did. A lot of huckleberries some days.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Right around that, right?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: We had wild huckleberries some days. You know, I grew them up in the woods. Small ones. Oh, we used to go and pick a lot of them. Small bushes, you know. We used to wild strawberries. We had a lot of fun up there. We went out in the woods and played in the woods. We had houses up in the woods. We'd come down there and things would grow on the trees, what do you call them? They'd fall off in the trees.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Oh, pine cones?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Yeah. Played with pine cones and made houses on the ground. We called it made houses, you know. They made houses like that with pine cones. I remember we did that too. We walked all around the country up there. We wanted to go someplace.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Now when this Big Anderson came to visit, he said that he had such a long reach to go across the table and everything.

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Yeah. He just stood up and reached across the whole table and he wanted something. The table wasn't so wide, though, you know. It was never long in there.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did he tell you any good stories? I understand he was supposed to have been able to tell good stories.

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: I suppose. I don't know what he told me. No, I couldn't tell you anything about that. No, he wasn't afraid of them. No, we wasn't afraid of them. When I went to school, there used to be a man come with a bunch of dogs, you know. We called him Wild Dave. Wild Dave, and he lived far up in the country, part country. He'd come everywhere once the pile went by there and we was afraid of him.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: What did he look like?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Long hair, really long hair, long whiskers. He'd come with a long string of dogs every once in a while. I don't know what he used to do. We were kind of afraid of him, though. We had to go through the woods to school all the time, you know. We never saw anything, no bad animals or anything. We never saw a coyote or nothing. We heard him at night. Sometimes the tree, it blew awful hard up there. Sometimes the tree blew right across the road. Well, I had to go with a saw and axe and take the tree away from the road. Yeah. That happened a lot of times.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: That would be on your own homestead where he kept the roads clear?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: No, it went through the pasture. We had to go through other people's pastures to get to the schoolhouse. We had to walk quite a ways. The tree blew over the road sometimes. People couldn't go through it when they saw the dogs away. But we never got hit by any trees. We were afraid to go through the woods. It lowered like everything and the trees fell down sometimes. It lowered them across the roads. Nothing ever happened to any of us. Ten of us in the family. Never happened to anything. Nothing bad. I'm always sure lucky. Never was sick, never even had sickness or anything. Sure thing.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did she have any kind of special medicine for you if you had colds or stuff like that?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: We treated her well. Homemade medicine. We never bought medicine in the States.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: What kind of medicine was that?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Lard. ... smeared all over her chest… that helped.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did it?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Did that for my kids too. I remember my husband did. Opened down the load. Coal oil sometimes makes it up with coal oil. I don't know how to help me get them these. Made cough medicine themselves. Made their own cough medicine.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: What did they make it out of?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: I don't know what they made it out of. Water and sugar and some kind of stuff they bought in the store. They mixed it up with water. That's good stuff too. Made their own cough medicine. They didn't go to town and buy everything in them days. And they bought groceries. So they lasted a long time when you go there when you left up there. We didn't go to town very often. Big sacks of flour. 100 pound sacks of flour. That didn't last too long.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: It didn't?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: We had to buy a sack every week I think.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Really?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Seemed like it. Big clotted bread for 10 children. Sometimes my mother baked bread before we went to school in the morning. And we had to take some more bread with us to school. That must have tasted good. You know when Nita's up in the morning and I baked before we went to school. Just think what it would have been like to do it today. No wonder your mother was so quiet. Yeah sure. She just discussed it I guess. ... She wasn't such a smart woman. She never made it. She had a lot of little clever shortcuts and stuff. Well she did with everything she made. She couldn't make everything you know. She couldn't buy all the clothes you know before the apartment. She bought interior and made the clothes. That helped like everything you know. I bought everything for my kids too. I didn't know how to sew. But I used to get a lot of hand-me-downs.

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: We never learned to sew anything.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did she sew by hand? You know she had a machine?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh yeah. She could sew by hand too. Oh she always had to thread the machine. ... She didn't have so many kinds of food to eat either. We didn't know any food. All kinds. We didn't know everything like they have nowadays. But we had good food. We were always healthy.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: That's what counts.

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: I was really lucky. The 10 of us was always healthy. I never was sick like a Mary and I had all kinds of problems. I don't know how to live everything then. I lived through all of it then. I never was sick when I was a girl. I didn't know what it was to be sick. That's marvelous. Yes it was. I never was sick.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Well when people did get sick on homesteads, did people stay away from them or did they go help them? How did it work?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh yeah they helped each other. That's what they did.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: So like with the measles or something they'd end up passing around wouldn't they?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: No that was no danger to some of these. Measles. I remember when I had the measles. My eyes were all the sort of I remember. There was a danger some days for the measles. More serious than was then. No. My mom sure was funny. I'm pretty sure she lived through it.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Sturdy stock as they say.

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Yeah, sure was. Everybody had big families. 11 by 11, 12 kids.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Were the young girls anxious to get married and have their own families?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: I don't know.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Most of them? I know you said you had too much fun. You waited.

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Not too much fun. I didn't care to get married.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: But most of your girlfriends in your age, were they getting married real early?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Yeah they got married earlier than I did.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: But not like 16, 17 and stuff.

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: I don't think they were that young. My sister was pretty young when they had to go to Spokane and work. They made it alright.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: You just get on the train and go?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Yeah, we come to go and took the train down here to Depot.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you have a job set up before you left? Did you have a job waiting?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: No, we went there to the employment office when I come to Spokane and look for a job. Went to employment office. They sent you to that place. Look at the bus. Streetcars. I always had nice places. Even to the bus. They cried when I left sometimes. I remember they cried when I left. I had nice places. And I was all small. They never made me work very hard. Oh, thank you. I was small. They always lived small for me. Smaller. Smaller. So I never had to work very hard. But I would have closed my hands. That's funny. People didn't even have washing machines when I worked there. I had to work and run by hand. We had double tubs though, you know.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: And washboards... What kind of soap did you use?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh, we used homemade soap sometimes up at the farm. My mother made it, but that's where I worked. It's Spokane. We used some hard soap, I think. I don't know what it was called. They waited to use powder them days, I think. We used to have bars of soap, you know, bar soap. Big bars. Rub that bar on the coast and then we'd rub it.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: But your mother made her own soap, huh?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Yeah, sometimes. Your mother was quite a worker. She milked the cows. She sure was. Whatever the bell meant to cows. I didn't want to milk the cows either.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Oh, you didn't?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: I'd go out and pick the little bit and I'd go out there running. Well, I didn't like to milk cows. I didn't have to do that much. Oh. No, my mother had to do that. I don't know who done it when she got sick though. I don't know who done it then… don't you remember… no, I never cared to milk any cows. I was afraid of the cows.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you have a lot of horses around the place?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: No, we never had many of them. Four of them, I think. Yeah. It was horses and geese on the fields, you know. But there were horses. Worked with the hans and the hie and everything.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: But do you remember your school very much?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh, yes, I remember school. We used to play better and put them in there. We played drop the handkerchief along the round and round. We played ball and softball, you know.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Oh, yeah?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: We played ball and just games, you know. We played ball and waded and barefooted sometimes.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Oh, yeah?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Because all of our shoes and talkies went to the creek. The schoolhouse was close to the creek. We had a lot of fun in the creek. Sure, we'd walk barefooted. Take off our shoes and talkies. Go to the creek and have fun. And they picked wild huckleberries, I mean gooseberries. We had wild gooseberries up around there. We were drowning to go to that bush, I remember, in recess. We had to take the birds. Yeah, we had to. We'd hurry to that bush and pick some gooseberries. It was good, too.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did your teacher let you speak Swedish in school?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: No.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: No?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: No, we had to learn English. Uh-huh. That didn't take long to learn English, I don't think. I don't know how we ever learned it, either. I'm not sure it seems funny.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: It just kind of happened, huh? Did you have the same teacher all the time?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh, no, we had different teachers. I remember I was awfully good to spell in school. I got surprises all the time. Oh. That was really good to spell. I never was. I can spell good yet. I can spell better than my young sisters can. I notice they can spell as good as I can. They may have spelled a lot of words, I noticed, in my letters. I hardly ever, ever forget to spell. I can spell all kinds of words.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did they teach spelling differently than they do now?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: When they got up in the long row and they spelled out, you know, one after another. They just keep spelling. I needed to draw maps on the board.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: I remember school, what do you call that, blackboard?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Uh-huh. I just copied from the one that stood next to me. Oh.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: I didn't know how to draw copies of different states, you know?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh. By heart… oh, I hated that. I just drew, looked at her and drew the best I could. Ah.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you ever get caught?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: My neighbor girl is a fan. She was really smart. Oh. She was mad when I got the prize and she got to be a school teacher too. She was jealous. She didn't like it. I didn't like that that I got the prize in school. She gets a man because I won… and she didn't.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Oh, was that in the spelling bee or?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Yeah, in the spelling bee. When you graduated. Oh, in the spelling bee. I wish I'd saved all the prizes I used to get from school. We've been friends and looked at them now. What kind of... I don't remember what all they got either. Oh. I can't remember that.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: But you got lots of them, huh?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: I thought it was fun to spell.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: That make you want to respond to that?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: I was good at reading and spelling and writing. That's what I was good at. I didn't care for the others. We learned so we got along. That's all we needed. We learned to read and write and to figure. We didn't need no education.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: We had to get out from work, didn't we?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Yeah. We couldn't stay home. We had to get out from work. They didn't send us to school like they do in others. We couldn't afford it.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Well, how long did you go to school?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: I don't remember how long I went to school either. My brother doesn't remember. I don't remember at all how many years we went to school.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: But then right after you got out of school, you had to go to work, huh?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Yeah, as soon as we was old enough to go to work, we had to get out of bed. And we had to learn our own clothes. We had to send home somebody. Two or five dollars a week is all I earned. Once I got six dollars a week.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: A week?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: We charged them by the month we paid it that way. Wow. I charged the store paid so much down there. The clothes was cheap them days. That was old pig… i missed him.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: That's your brother, huh?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: ... My brother lives down there on the east street. Well, that's right. He should be here today and tell you everything. He can tell you lots of things. I don't know who to tell him.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Sam's talked to him.

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Sam?

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: He's my boss. He's talked to your brother. I listened to a little bit of your brother's tape where he was talking about Big Anderson.

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: That's what made me think of asking you if you remembered him. Yeah, I remembered him. He used to come by our place for Never Sunday when he went to church.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: And he'd walk all that way?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: He'd come in the house because he's talking to us about it. Oh, it's terrible. Big man, he was awful big. Big long stick in his hand.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: The stick was to help him walk?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Yeah, to help his legs. He had some kind of disease in his legs in August. It's terrible. He lived there anyway. He didn't die for, he lived there for many years, I think. I don't know how long he lived there. Big Anderson.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: He was dug out.

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: He looked at you all kinds of things.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: He was saying something about a machine or an invention or something like that?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Yeah, maybe he'd done something like that. Had some kind of a machine. I don't know what he'd done, maybe.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: You remember him being real friendly?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh yeah, I guess he was. But he didn't dare to eat the stuff that they brought him, though, they said, because he was afraid they'd bring him something that he'd get sick from. No, he didn't like it, he didn't like that.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: But he ate at your house?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh yeah, he ate at our house. He wasn't afraid to eat at our house, but I think I heard that when people brought him stuff he didn't dare to eat it. Well, maybe they were going to kill him, you know. He'd get sick from it. Maybe he was worried about that. Apparently.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Oh, you remember the kind of spreads your mother used to put out for Sunday dinner?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh, just plain food.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Just plain food, huh?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: I guess you ate the same potato sausage and may have always had potatoes and that's supposed to be neat. She was good to make cakes and she could make pies. We didn't eat that, we didn't eat that. We ate that.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Oh yeah?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: We ate a big, we bought the big sacks of oatmeal, you know, big bags, you know, but pretty big bags of oatmeal, you know. We ate that mostly, I think. Oatmeal.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Would that be like for your supper or for your breakfast?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: All for breakfast. You were talking about the big stack of pancakes. We had company. My mother always fixed up more than we did for our whole family. We had company a lot, too. It was great to go from place to place, you know, and have dinners. Yeah. We was invited out many times here and there around the country. You don't do that, nowadays. Not too much. We thought that was fine. We'd always go and have good dinners. We went out to clear to Moscow sometime. We as kids had been on the way. We survived there. Toward Moscow. Family that my folks knew. I remember that, too. There was a long ways to drive in that number wagon. I bet it was. Up to Moscow. Nine miles up there and then Troy and up to Moscow. We had a lot of fun going to history. Stayed all night sometimes. We had a lot of fun. That's the way they did that day. Went home in the morning.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you have lots of people come visit you, too?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh, yes, we had. We had some big families come to our place, too. There was a lot of work from my mother, too, in our place for extra people. We kids had to wait. We didn't have enough chairs and we had to wait until they were through evening. We made the kids wait some days.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Oh, yeah, the kids didn't go first like they didn't have, huh?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: No… they didn't do that some days. We always had special ones in that company. They were great that we'd go together and eat. That was fun. People come and visit in the evening with a lantern in their hand. A long ways to come and visit in the evening. Huh. That's what they did. They took the lantern in their hand and they would come and walk. That was their entertainment, visiting. Yeah, coming and visiting in the evening. We thought that was great when somebody would come and visit in the evening. It was awesome to sit up there.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: I guess it would be. Did your dad have to work real hard?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh, yes, he worked pretty hard. Had to work hard them days. Yeah.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Was he just a farmer or did he do something else?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: He made it all right. Ten children. Yeah. He was married three times. Oh, my goodness. That's why I got stepbrothers and step-brothers. Step-sisters and one half-brother. Well, it was just Philip .... One of the me. My other sister's living in Spokane. One in Massachusetts.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Oh, my goodness. She got far away.

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Had two sisters in Spokane and one in Massachusetts. Uh-huh. And one up in Wenatchee. I have a two-father. Yeah. My sisters in Spokane, they come up to see me. They come up here to see me. Had a lot of relations in Spokane… nieces and sisters… nephews and...

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: When people come visiting, would they just sit around and talk?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: They just sit around and talk. Play cards or games or... Had to have lunch in the afternoon after the dinner. They gave them lunch, put them at home. Always eat twice.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: The main thing was eating then, huh?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Yeah, it was the main thing. We didn't have any music at home, though. We just sat around and talked. Kids played outside. Go fishing in the summer. Wasn't far to run down the creek. We had a lot of fun.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did you have any other kind of special games that you played?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: No, I don't know. I can't think of any other. We didn't have much movies. No music in the house or anything, no. We had some people there, I guess. I went past them.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did it?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: You had a lot of work to do in between, I guess. We spent a lot longer than that. We did a lot of things some days.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did your mom do canning and things like that?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Oh, yes… we like to do the ridges. We got a lot of prunes, big, big. The tub was full of prunes and candy.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Prunes?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Prunes. Somebody had an orchard. We didn't have an orchard at home very much. No, we didn't have that much. We went to the farmers and got them. We didn't have to pay much for them either. It was cheap, at least. Oh, yes, you can. But you didn't have much vegetables. We had other vegetables. We had celery and kept them in the cellar. We had a lot of fruits. We had apples and apple sauce. We didn't eat too many kinds of fruit, did we? Apples and fruits. We had a pair of orchards and got pears. Little berries out here. We had pears a lot of times.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: The whole family would go and pick the fruit or did the farmer have it picked for you?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: I wonder, we went and picked our own. You thought it was fun, we could go to the orchards and pick stuff.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Well, tell me some more about when you'd hike into town to Troy here for the dances. I thought that was neat.

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: We'd lunch along and stuff down the road and ate some lunch. That's what we did. Boy, that's a long distance. Nine miles to walk. That's fine, I like to walk. I wish I could be that kid.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Were there a lot of kids that did this?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: I don't know… we decided it was just too long and we went. Uh-huh. It was safe for two girls to just go like that. Oh yes, we never was afraid of anybody on the road. Nobody hurt anybody nowadays. No, there was nothing happening around there. No danger around there. No danger by animals or anything nowadays. We heard the coyotes hollering and hollering at night there. We didn't cheat. Sometimes we'd see them on the field, but we never saw them go to school. They'd run across and run the field sometimes.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: They never known to hurt anybody though, were they?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: No, no, we never got hurt. We never played with any of them. And bears. Never saw a bear around there either.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: What about Troy? When you got into Troy, what was it like?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: There wasn't many buildings. Some days. I've heard some things like there was a saloon every other door and things like this. Yeah, I've heard.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Is that right?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: I guess it was. Boy, he'd buy some whiskey sometimes. He used that for medicine. Oh. Yeah, he used that when he had a coat. Oh. That's all he used it for. Yeah.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Did he let the kids have it for a cold?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: No. I don't know if he did or not.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: At least he didn't let you.

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: My brothers, they found out enough when they got older. Found out about that later. ... Boy, we're driving all kinds of bad roads. All the roads are bad. Horses have to jump over the ditches all the time. Hmm. Not a bad road some days. There's no roads like they have now days.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Who was it that fixed the roads? Kept them up?

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: One of the farmers. Went to heaven. Hmm. But they had to go out to fix them. They were a hassle. You can handle a big machine or something like that. They have .... They're for .... Hmm. I don't know how they fixed the road. I think it has the trillings. Alina, are you in there? I thought she was in there. No, I think she left the papers and snuck out. Well, don't worry about it. She's sitting there as a quiet.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: Yeah, she's not that quiet, huh? Well, maybe I better get going for today.

speaker: Amanda Asplund Phelan or Addie Swanson
words: Yeah, I don't think you'll find out very much from me. Have a good time. You know, I've been here over an hour. Well, yeah, I'm good class. We got somebody to help you out. Oh, yeah. Yeah, she says she goes up.

speaker: Karen Purtee
words: I mean, you were the one that put the news in the paper, huh?

speaker: Unknown Speaker
words: Yeah… yeah. One time. And someone, I think, maybe someone kind of smiled at him. Well, he laughed too. He said, you know, most everybody's life is interesting. Their life story. Even yours. He said it to that person.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: So you think ...?

speaker: Unknown Speaker
words: Mine would be interesting too. I bet you would be too. Even as a young man. If you could just hit enough high spots close enough, not skip two longer spaces in between, it would be interesting too. It's funny. I think about that now and then, but I don't think I have my story down yet. I think maybe when I've lived a lot longer, I will. Yeah, yeah. Yes, you will. But now it doesn't seem very interesting. Well, some things aren't interesting. When I think of some of the hardships I went through, I remember one time, one year, I remember one year, and that was then the fella's fault, but mine too. I ought to have more sense. I had a cousin that always, he didn't care how hard the other fella had. He just didn't care how hard the job was, or working for him. He just didn't care. You want another fella to do most of the work, that's it. And I went to work for him one time, him and his brother-in-law. Oh, they had a lot of land. And I went to shock and grain for him. And you know, a man does good when he keeps up with one binder. Shock and grain.

speaker: Unknown Speaker
words: You don't know much about binders though, do you?

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Just seeing pictures of them.

speaker: Unknown Speaker
words: Yeah, yeah. Well, they drop out bundles. You have to pick them up and shock them. And that's a man's job. When a man does that, he's done a hard day's work. You know what they had me do? Keep up with two binders. Yeah, and I was just about 18 or 19 years old. And because they knew I'd do it, they had me do it. They said, take it easy, do what you ought to. But they just had me do it, yeah. And things like that, when I think of it, there's not very many people who'd have a boy doing that. He was a good fella every other way too. Everybody liked him. And I just... He just took advantage of you. Yeah, yeah, yeah.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Boy, that sounds tough.

speaker: Unknown Speaker
words: Well, so many young fellas, when they become 21 years old or older, was coming west to the lower land. So, the fellas back in the Hong-Nam times, they liked it too. Of course, it was more wild and wooly then too, but they liked it a lot better than they did back east.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: I don't know if it's a certain kind of people that like it out here, and there's others that don't want to change, or what the reason is that some people come out and some people stay.

speaker: Unknown Speaker
words: Yeah, but I tell you, there's not very many people that were born back east and come out here and live here a while. They don't want to go back. I think the percentage is pretty small. But, I never did see the time that I ever wanted to live. After World War I, I was married back east and we stayed back there a year or two afterwards. And I never had a week to go back to this place. I'd like to go back and visit.

speaker: Sam Schrager
words: Would you want to live there?

speaker: Unknown Speaker
words: No, I wouldn't want to at all. No sir.
